en: A Concise Compendium on the Śrāmaṇerī Vinaya Rules, compiled by the śramaṇa Duti, Director of Vinaya Studies at Longchang Temple on Mount Hua. *Śrāmaṇerī*:

This is translated into Chinese as "the girl who has stilled [evil] and embraced [kindness]" (*xící nǚ*). It means to cease unwholesome conduct and cultivate compassion; to cease worldly defilements and...
She is one who compassionately benefits sentient beings. She is also called a *śrāmaṇerī* (female diligent practitioner) or a *śikṣamāṇā* (female seeker of tranquility).
Regarding "vinaya" (discipline), it refers to the ten precepts and various codes of dignified conduct.

In the section on the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts within the Vinaya Gate of the preceding volume, the Buddha said: "Those aged sixteen or above should become *śrāmaṇerī*s. [Original text fragment ends here.]

One who is free from blemish, upright and virtuous, and complete in all respects; one who has not suffered any disgrace or humiliation; and one whose parents have granted permission—such a person may become a practitioner of the Way.

One who is not naturally upright and virtuous should not become a practitioner of the Way. A stone statue or one afflicted by parasites should not become a practitioner of the Way, for the feminine disposition is difficult to preserve:
delight lasts but a moment, and evil thoughts arise again, like a bubble of water that forms and then vanishes.
It is extinguished; there is no permanent stability. One must observe carefully before ordaining a nun.
Furthermore, the Buddha beheld that from the human realm up to the twenty-eighth heaven and down to the eighteen hells, all is suffering with no joy.

Thus, he established the precepts to instruct future generations. Consequently, laywomen who shave their heads and leave the household life first receive the ten branches of prohibitory precepts, which are called—
The rules for her are the same as those for a śrāmaṇerikā. Next, she is granted two years to undergo training in the six dharmas and becomes a śikṣamāṇā.

Once these years are completed and she has mastered the purifications, becoming fit to enter the ranks of the subordinate saṃgha, she shall request and receive the bhikṣuṇī precepts within the assembly of the two-fold saṃgha;
this is indeed the correct regulation. Lately, however, the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya has lost its fundamental principle, and contemporary customs have fallen into decline, such that even śrāmaṇeras...

As for the nuns themselves, they are not yet familiar with the precepts they have originally received; those who are arrogant often slight the Great Sangha of both divisions, while those who are ignorant completely lose sight of the subtle practices of all the gates.
To desire to illuminate the transformation of the Path in order to guide the assembly of nuns is something difficult to hope for.

Therefore, I have selected the ten precepts to briefly clarify their prohibitions, so that those who study them may know the direction toward which they should turn. May those who have left the household life with a sincere heart [attain this].
Apply your whole mind to its practice and be careful not to transgress it. For in the near term, it serves as the ladder for the śikṣamāṇā and the bhikṣuṇī precepts;
in the distant term, it is the foundation of the bodhisattva precepts. Through the precepts, concentration arises; through concentration, wisdom is developed.
May you thus achieve the holy path and not fail the original aspiration that led you to leave the household life.
Those who delight in extensive reading should, of course, examine the complete canon of the Vinaya in detail.
The following ten precepts are extracted verbatim from the relevant fascicles of the Vinaya Piṭaka, without any addition or omission.
First: The Precept Against Killing.

The first precept for a śrāmaṇerī: One must not kill living beings. One should have compassion for all creatures, cherishing them as parents cherish their children, and extend pity to even the wriggling insects as if they were infants.
What is meant by "not killing"? It is to guard one’s body, speech, and mind. With the body, one does not kill humans, animals, or any crawling or breathing creatures;

one does not do so with one's own hands, nor does one incite others to do so. Upon seeing that a being has been killed, one does not eat it; upon hearing that a being has been killed, one does not [eat it].
One should not eat meat that has been killed out of doubt; one should not eat meat killed for one's sake. One must not say with one's mouth, "I shall kill," "I shall harm," or "I shall take revenge.
Nor should one say, "Death is a pleasure," "Killing is a pleasure," "So-and-so is fat," "So-and-so is thin," or "The meat of so-and-so is good," or "The meat of so-and-so is poor."
Furthermore, one should not harbor thoughts such as, "I shall rob, kill, or slaughter such-and-such a person; it would be a pleasure," nor should one think of fattening or emaciating certain beings.
One should pity all sentient beings as if they were one's own marrow, as if they were one's father or mother, as if they were one's child or one's own body—equal and without distinction.
With universal equanimity and a single mind, one should always be intent upon the Mahāyāna. This is the novice nun’s initial training in the precepts.
The second precept for stealing, the śrāmaṇerī precept: One must not steal anything worth one *kākiṇī* or more. One must not take grass, leaves, hair, or rice.

If the owner does not give it with their own hand, one must not take it. One must not speak of taking it with the mouth, nor think of taking it with the mind, nor gaze upon it with longing in the eyes. Nor [with the ears...]
The ear does not crave sound; the nose does not steal fragrance; the tongue does not pilfer flavor; the body does not covet clothing; the mind does not pilfer desire.
When the six sense-faculties are free from attachment and one constantly establishes skillful means and wisdom, this is called "not stealing. This constitutes the precept for a śrāmaṇerikā.

The third precept for śrāmaṇerikās regarding sexual misconduct: One must not engage in lewdness. What is meant by non-lewdness? It is true singularity and purity. To keep the body clean and free from lewdness;
not to speak of lewdness with the mouth; and not to think of lewdness with the mind. To maintain oneself with such clarity as the wind in space, which has nothing upon which to rely.

He is detached. His body does not engage in lust; his eyes do not gaze lustfully; his ears do not listen lustfully; his nose does not seek lustful fragrances; his mouth does not speak lustful words; and his mind harbors no desire.
He contemplates that the four great elements of the body are fundamentally non-existent. Calculating earth, water, fire, and wind, he finds no self, no person, no life-span, and no soul.
What is there to be lustful toward? What is there to be attached to? His will is fixed upon emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. This is [the practice].
This is the precept for śrāmaṇerikās.
Fourth, the precept against false speech:

a śrāmaṇerikā must not engage in double-tongued speech or harsh words; her speech should be composed and serene. If she has not seen something, she must not say that she saw it. If she has not... [seen it], she must not say that she saw it.
Upon hearing something, do not speak of it; upon seeing evil, do not transmit it; upon hearing evil, do not proclaim it; avoid evil words directly.

Constantly practice the four immeasurables and refrain from improper speech. Whenever you speak, always discourse on the Path; do not discuss worldly matters, nor speak of kings, ministers, officials, or bandits.
Constantly extol the sutras and dharmas and the correct precepts of the Bodhisattvas. Set your mind upon the Mahāyāna and do not engage in the study of the Lesser Vehicle. Practice the four...
Equanimity: these constitute the precepts for a śrāmaṇerī (*zhí bì bié běn jūn zuò zhēn pì; now corrected according to the Goryeo ancient edition*).
Fifth, the precept against drinking alcohol:
a śrāmaṇerī must not drink alcohol, must not crave alcohol, and must not taste alcohol. There are thirty [types of] alcohol.
There are six losses. Losing the Way and destroying the family; endangering the person and forfeiting one’s life—all of these arise from this.

Being pulled east and dragged west, held south and bound north, one cannot recite the sutras, does not revere the Triple Gem, treats teachers and friends with contempt, and is unfilial toward one’s parents.

With the mind closed and the intellect obstructed, one remains ignorant from lifetime to lifetime, failing to encounter the Great Way. Because the mind lacks discernment, one must abstain from drinking alcohol, desiring to remain free from [these faults].
The five aggregates, the five desires, the six hindrances, attaining the five supernatural powers, and crossing over the five paths— these constitute the precepts for a śrāmaṇerikā.
The sixth is the precept against being attached to incense, flowers, and necklaces.
The Precepts for Śrāmaṇerikās: One must not wear fragrant flowers to scent or adorn oneself. One’s robes, coverlets, shoes, and sandals must not be of five colors.
One must not ornament oneself with various jewels. One must not wear brocade, embroidery, silk gauze, or fine silks. One must not gaze with a flirtatious expression;
one should instead wear coarse clothing—blue, black, madder-brown, or the saffron-colored inner robe—and walk with the head bowed, desiring to eliminate [defilements].
Regarding the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one takes precepts as fragrance; seeking to recite the profound Dharma, one regards it as the truth; taking the thirty-two marks as necklaces;

and attaining the cultivation of the various secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), one regards them as garments. One vows that the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) be unimpeded, and that the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) guide all beings.
These are the precepts for śrāmaṇerikās.
The seventh is the precept against sitting on high, wide, or large beds;
it is a śrāmaṇerikā precept that one must not sit upon beds made of gold or silver, nor upon those with embroidered silks, brocades, or various precious coverlets.
Maintain mindfulness. Do not seek out fine beds, couches, mats, five-colored painted fans, or superior whisks.

Do not wear armlets or finger-rings. With true faith, precepts, shame, remorse, generosity, extensive learning, wisdom, single-minded concentration, and constant pursuit of samādhi, take these as your bed and couch.
With an unshakable mind and the spontaneous arising of manifold wisdom, take these as your seat.
Endowed with these, the seven factors of enlightenment do not waver, and one is intent upon the mind of the Way; this constitutes the śrāmaṇerī precepts.
The eighth is the śrāmaṇerī precept against dancing, singing, and music:
one must not listen to the sounds of dancing, singing, or music, nor clap hands or beat time to the rhythm, nor perform such acts oneself.
Nor does he instruct others; he constantly cultivates his own person, practices the True Dharma in accordance with it, and refrains from unwholesome conduct.

With a single mind he takes refuge in the Buddha, reciting the sutras and practicing the Right Path, taking this as his dharma-joy rather than worldly pleasure. He listens to the sutras and reflects upon them, penetrating deeply into their great meaning.

Unless she is ill, she must not ride in carriages, on horses, or on elephants; rather, she should contemplate lightness and elevation, taking the attainment of inconceivable supernormal powers as her vehicle to cross over and be liberated from the eight difficulties. This is the precept for a śrāmaṇerikā.

The ninth is the precept of not grasping or possessing gold and jewels, a śrāmaṇerikā precept. One must not accumulate precious treasures; one must not take them with one's own hands; one must not instruct others to do so.

One should always be single-mindedly diligent, regarding the Way as treasure, the Sūtras as supreme, and the meaning [of the teachings] as wondrous, understanding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

This is the foundation. As for the three liberations, one does not seek after sensual desire. Wishing to be free from the nine afflictions, one dwells in the Path for a very long time—without end, without limit, and without boundary—and yet remains in no fixed abode. This is the precept of the śrāmaṇerī.
The tenth precept for śrāmaṇerikās is the precept against eating at improper times.
One must not lose the proper time for meals; one should always eat at the appropriate time and must not exceed the limit by eating after midday.

One must not eat again. Even if there are sweet and exquisite flavors beyond measure, one shall never eat them again, nor shall one teach others to transgress this, nor even entertain such thoughts in the mind. Even if the unsurpassed, spontaneous food were to come, it must not be eaten.
If a householder or a king offers food after midday has passed, one shall not eat it either; until death, one shall not transgress, constantly contemplating meditative concentration. One.
Regarding all food and drink: although she consumes them, she does so merely to sustain her life.
She desires that all beings may understand profound vows and attain the ten powers as their sustenance. This is the precept for a śrāmaṇerikā.

In the lower section, the Gate of Dignified Conduct (*īryāpatha*), it is stated that the Buddha established the rules for the community of nuns; the discipline (*vinaya*) for the great assembly of monks is even more rigorous, as the True Dharma depends upon whether it increases or diminishes. A detailed examination of the Sage’s...
The regulations for this are clear. If a śrāmaṇerī does not know what she ought to perform, she is not permitted to receive full ordination (upasaṃpadā).
Because the duties of a fully ordained bhikṣuṇī are even more difficult to carry out, she must be made to study them thoroughly until she understands them;

only then may she be allowed to receive the complete precepts. If one were to grant her the full precepts while she is still ignorant, it would imply that the Buddha-dharma is easy to practice, which is a grave error.
The monastic community is easy to establish. Therefore, a śrāmaṇerī should first honor the training.

The following articles are extracted from the *Mahāprajāpatī Sūtra*, the *Śrāmaṇerī-śikṣāpada-vinaya*, and the second section on the "Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya-vidhi" (the rules of deportment for bhikṣuṇīs). They are also found in Yunqi’s *Essentials for Śrāmaṇeras*.

Within this collection, all that is generally applicable to śrāmaṇerīs has likewise been gathered. This is because, in this age of the Dharma’s decline, the nuns’ dispositions are often characterized by indolence;
they grow weary when hearing too much, and there is a constant fear that their understanding may become superficial due to excessive textual detail.

Therefore, the redundant has been deleted and the essentials extracted, further organized into categories to facilitate study. Where there were occasional omissions, they have been supplemented according to the meaning.
Enter into the first and second [sections]. Those who delight in broad learning should naturally examine the complete text themselves.
First among the three objects of veneration, one must revere the Buddha.
With a sincere mind free from deceit, prostrate with the head touching the ground, and constantly repent of the evils and sins committed in past lives.
○ Always revere the Dharma. Keep the Way in mind and show compassionate filiality toward the sutras. ○ Always revere the Sangha.
Maintain an impartial mind without negligence, being most sincere and faithful. ○ One must not, on account of a minor matter, become angry and abandon the Triple Gem.
○ One must not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecation or urination. ○ One must not enter a Buddha hall or a monastery stupa wearing impure footwear.
Beginning from the time of leaving home and receiving the precepts, throughout the remainder of one's life, one should at all times maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
Morning and evening, one should prostrate to the Buddha and make this vow: "In every place where I am born, may I possess the marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa) and leave home as a celibate youth."

One should immediately be able to draw near to the Triple Gem, making offerings and serving them. Regarding women living nearby as well as in the presence of donors, one should praise the merits of the Triple Gem to increase their faith.
Whenever one wears a single garment, eats a single meal, or drinks a single draught, one should never forget the Buddha’s kindness.
When putting on new clothes or shoes, one should first pay homage to the Buddha; when receiving food and drink, [one should likewise do so].
First, one should make offerings to the Buddha; always maintain a sense of shame and remorse; give rise to thoughts of contentment;
and respect the Great Śramaṇas (the second [category]: the Great Śramaṇas refers to both Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs, as this collectively encompasses the two divisions of the Great Saṃgha).
One must not address the two divisions of the Great Saṃgha by their personal names. One must not eavesdrop on the two divisions of the Great Saṃgha while they are reciting the precepts.
One must not go about spreading reports of the faults of the two assemblies of great monks.

One must not fail to rise when seeing the two assemblies of great monks, except during the time of reciting scriptures, when ill, when shaving the head, at mealtime, or while performing communal duties.
One must not intentionally use strange speech to provoke or disturb the two assemblies of great monks. One must not groundlessly slander the two assemblies of great monks out of anger.

○ One must not incite discord between the two assemblies of the great Sangha. ○ One must not intentionally harass the two assemblies of the great Sangha under the pretext of inquiring about the Sūtras and Vinaya.
○ One must not revile the two assemblies of the great Sangha. ○ One must not walk in front of the two assemblies of the great Sangha.
○ One must not treat the two assemblies of the great Sangha with contempt or intentionally joke and laugh in their presence.
One should imitate their speech, appearance, and manner of walking. One must not, when observing the two divisions of the Great Sangha passing by in a secluded place, point at their backs.
When walking and encountering the two divisions of the Great Sangha, one should immediately step off the path, lower one’s head, and stand to the side with respectful deference;
only after they have passed may one proceed.
Regarding the third matter of serving one’s teacher:
view the Upādhyāya and Ācārya as you would the Buddha. One should revere the teacher and always remain close to them, acting in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya.
One should follow the teacher’s instructions and always remain harmonious and compliant. One should always rise early and never be later than the teacher.

One should admonish one’s own mind so as not to cause the teacher to call out. ○ When rising early, one should first purify oneself, don the dharma robes, pay homage to the Buddha and the Dharma, and then pay homage to the teacher.

○ When wishing to enter a room, one should first snap the fingers three times. ○ When paying homage to the teacher, one should stand six feet away, inquire after his well-being, and then withdraw and exit the room.
○ One should not prostrate when the teacher is sitting in meditation. One should not [prostrate] when the teacher is walking in meditation.
One should not perform prostrations when the teacher is eating, combing his teeth, bathing, or sleeping.

○ If one wishes to prostrate and the teacher stops them, one should obey the command and refrain from bowing. ○ When the teacher has closed the door, one should not perform prostrations outside the door.
If one wishes to enter the room to prostrate, one should snap the fingers three times; if the teacher does not respond, one should depart. ○ If [the teacher] sends...
When emptying the vessel for impurities, one must not spit, nor harbor anger. One should be sincere and faithful toward the teacher, serving him with all one’s heart.
One should be compassionate and filial toward the teacher, keeping him constantly in mind, never leaving his side even for eating or resting.

If, while traveling through the country, one encounters strange or extraordinary events, one should inform the teacher and inquire about the cause of such anomalies. When receiving the scriptures from the teacher, one should maintain a focused and upright mind.
This is the ultimate reality: body, speech, mind, and intention must not differ by even a hair’s breadth.
If your teacher sends you on an errand, you should go quickly and return quickly. If someone asks, "Śrāmaṇerikā, is your teacher there?", you should remain silent and proceed directly.
One must not be known to associate with [those who criticize the teacher]. ○ If there are faults or evils, one should immediately confess them to the teacher, saying, "I have acted without propriety.
○ One should place full trust in the teacher. If anyone speaks of the teacher's faults, one should immediately rebuke and stop them.

○ When carrying food or drink for the teacher, one should always support it with both hands. After the meal, when putting away the utensils, one should do so slowly. ○ In attending to the teacher, one must not...

Stand facing [the teacher]. Do not stand at a high elevation; do not stand too far away. You should position yourself so that the teacher’s low-voiced words can be heard without taxing his venerable strength.
If you wish to inquire about the Buddha-Dharma, you should adjust your robes, prostrate, join your palms, listen attentively, and contemplate deeply.
If you ask about matters of daily life, there is no need to prostrate; simply stand upright by the teacher’s side and speak according to the facts.
Shen said: "If the Master’s body or mind becomes weary, you should call him and he should go; you must not show displeasure in your heart or on your countenance.
You must not sit playfully upon the Master’s seat, nor lie down upon his bed, nor wear his robes or hat.
If the Master falls ill, you must attend to him from beginning to end, taking great care with every detail: the room, the bedding, the medicine, and the congee."

[These matters of] treatment, [as well as] holding robes, handing over sandals, washing and dyeing, drying and sunning, etc., are fully detailed in the Vinaya; they shall not be recorded here at length. In all cases of attending a teacher:
one must not sit unless commanded to do so, and one must not answer unless questioned. This applies except when one has a personal matter that one wishes to inquire about.

In all cases of standing in attendance: one must not lean against a wall or rest against a desk. One should maintain an upright posture with feet together and stand slightly to the side. [The Teacher...]

When given a task or command, one should perform it promptly and without delay; one must not be negligent or disrespectful. ○ Regarding sleep, one must not precede the teacher, except when there is a reason for illness;
in such cases, one must inform the teacher and receive his permission to rest. ○ When asked for one's name, one should say, "I am so-and-so by courtesy, and so-and-so by birth."
One must not sit or lie down before the teacher with legs crossed or hands on the hips. If the teacher rises while one is seated, one should immediately rise quickly upon being commanded to do so.
One should guard the teacher’s belongings as one would one's own life, and must not give them away privately to others.
One must not look at the teacher with a malicious gaze. One must not remain apart from the teacher on one's own unless the teacher has passed away or is otherwise preoccupied by circumstances.
If [the teacher] travels far away, you must not follow him. You should pay respects and inform your original teacher: "Upon whom should I rely for dependence?
You should act according to the teacher's instructions and then dwell in dependence upon that person. In all matters, the rules for living together with the teacher remain no different.

If the teacher passes away without having designated a successor, you must select another worthy guide and dwell in dependence upon them. If the teacher has broken the precepts, held wrong views, or been expelled by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma...
As when undergoing disciplinary measures such as *pravāsanīya-karman*, one must likewise seek out a learned master (*ācārya*) upon whom to rely for residence;
one must not act according to one's own whims. One must not reside relying on the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*). One must not live together with a novice (*śrāmaṇera*).

One must not follow the teacher to dwell or travel through scenic regions or flower gardens. One must not follow the teacher to dwell in shrines, cemeteries, or hermitages. Even if the teacher resides there, [one must not].
One should perform prostrations and offer admonitions according to the Vinaya. During the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should dwell near the boundary of a *mahā-bhikṣu* following one’s teacher;
one must not observe the summer retreat in a place where no *bhikṣu* resides. If the teacher has anything to bestow, one should receive it after respectfully prostrating;
if one already possesses it, one should say so, and must not accept it falsely.

Fourth, when following the teacher on an excursion, one must not pass through or visit private residences. One must not stop by the side of the road to converse with others. One must not look left or right;
rather, one should keep the head bowed and eyes level while following behind the teacher. Upon arriving at the house of a donor (*dānapati*), one should stand to one side.

When the teacher instructs one to sit, one shall then sit. ○ When visiting another temple, the teacher shall pay homage to the Buddha; or he may do so himself, but one must not strike the *qing* bell on one's own authority.

○ When the teacher receives a vegetarian meal offering (*zhāi*), one should stand by to offer the dedication of merit (*chūshēng*). Upon the conclusion of the meal, one should again attend him while standing to receive the monetary offerings (*qīn*).
○ If traveling for some reason, one should go accompanied by three others. ○ One should travel together with a senior nun (*dàní*). ○ If with a laywoman (*upāsikā*)...
Walking together: one should wear the dharma robes while walking. When putting on the robes, they should be properly adjusted.
One must not walk with the robes tucked over the shoulders. One must not walk with the robes wrapped around the neck. One must not walk by jumping. One must not walk with hands placed on the hips.
One must not walk by swaying the body. One must not walk by swinging the arms. One must not walk while laughing or joking. One should follow behind the teacher.
When walking, one must not step upon the teacher’s form or shadow. If one encounters flowers or fruit by the roadside, one must not pluck them at will.

Whether traveling far or near with the teacher, one must not utter words of resentment or speak of suffering, nor manifest signs of fatigue. If one encounters a man on the road, one must not look at him or dwell upon him;
one should contemplate emptiness and cultivate the perception of impurity. If one sees strange or unusual things of the mundane world along the way, [one should likewise remain detached].
One must not lose one's composure while offering praise.
Fifth, when entering the assembly, one must not dispute over one’s seat. One must not call out to, speak with, or laugh with others from their seats. Within the assembly...
To lose propriety is a transgression. One should conceal faults and promote virtues; one must not boast of one's own toil or manifest one's own merits.
○ One must not sit together with *mahābhikṣus* or *mahābhikṣuṇīs*. ○ One must not mock or laugh at one another. ○ One must not blow one's nose or spit loudly.
○ One must not relieve oneself on the four sides of a Buddha-stūpa, causing foul odors to enter. ○ Not...
One may defecate or urinate facing a Buddha stūpa. One must not sit with legs extended toward a Buddha stūpa.
When drinking tea or soup, one must not perform a prostration with only one hand. One must not speak excessively, laugh much, or yawn; one should cover the mouth with the sleeve of one’s robe.
Regarding flowers offered to the Buddha, select those that are fresh and full-blown; do not smell them first. Only after removing the withered ones should they be offered.
Regarding new items: one must not discard withered things on the ground or trample them; they should be placed in a secluded spot.
○ One should provide tooth-sticks and water for rinsing for the great bhikṣuṇīs according to one's ability; as soon as the opportunity arises, one should do so.

One must not seek ease through negligence, but should instead seek superior merit. ○ When hearing a call, one should immediately respond by reciting the Buddha’s name; one must not say "I am here" or "It is I. ○
Whenever one picks up a lost article, one must inform the administrative bhikṣuṇī. Whenever entering a Buddha hall, one must maintain a solemn demeanor;
one must not act with unrestrained license. One must not use harsh speech to mock others, nor teach others to speak unwholesome words.
One must not sit idly by while the assembly performs labor, avoiding work out of laziness or seeking personal ease. One must not privately take offerings.
Regarding bamboo, wood, flowers, fruits, vegetables, all food and drink, as well as all utensils and the like:
Whenever referring to oneself, one must cite one’s two-character dharma-name; one must not say "I" or "so-and-so. One must not engage in disputes over minor matters.
Even in cases of major matters that are difficult to endure, one must maintain a level mind and a harmonious temper, resolving them through reasoned argument; one must not [act otherwise].
Then one should take one's leave and depart. If the movement of the breath is coarse, one is not yet a śrāmaṇerī.

○ Upon entering the Great Sangha Hall, first pay homage to the image of the Holy Monk (Sengzhong), and then perform the prostrations to the ten directions. ○ If one sees a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇera, one should likewise pay them homage.
Sixth, regarding eating in accordance with the assembly:
upon hearing the sound of the *ghanṭā*, one should immediately adjust one’s robes. When about to eat, one should offer prayers for blessings and maintain reverence throughout.
Regarding the serving of food: rice shall not exceed seven grains; noodles shall not exceed one inch; and steamed buns shall not exceed the size of a fingernail. To exceed these amounts is improper.
If one is greedy, it becomes stinginess. Other vegetables and tofu are not served. Whenever food is brought out, silently recite this verse:
"O hosts of ghosts and spirits, I now bestow this offering upon you. This food pervades the ten directions; may all ghosts and spirits share in it.
Whenever eating and drinking, contemplate these five reflections: First, calculate the labor expended and measure the distance from which the food was brought.

2. Reflect upon one’s own virtue and conduct to determine whether one is worthy of the offering. 3. Guard the mind against faults, making the abandonment of greed and other afflictions the primary principle.

4. Properly regard the food as excellent medicine for healing the withered body. 5. Accept this food solely for the purpose of attaining the Way. ○ Do not criticize the quality of the food, whether it be good or bad.
○ One must not privately give away any portion of the food; even if one picks out a bit to give to a dog, this is forbidden. ○ When someone comes to add more food, one must not refuse.

Do not speak [while eating]. If you are already full, you should signal this by waving your hand back. ○ Do not pick at the head of the food with your fingernails, causing crumbs to fall into the neighboring bowls.
○ Do not speak while holding food in your mouth. ○ Do not engage in laughter, chatter, or idle conversation. ○ Do not make noise while chewing your food.

The Ritual for the Recitation of the Precepts.
On the fifteenth day of both the waxing and waning moon, at dawn, the administrative official reports to the Abbot: "Today we shall recite the precepts.

The Abbot then instructs an attendant to summon the secretary to draft an invitation slip for the *kalyāṇamitra* (preceptor). The administrative official delivers the slip to the *kalyāṇamitra*'s quarters.
Upon his arrival, the official bows in greeting and departs, instructing the duty officer to strike the bell—or alternatively, the drum three times—in front of the Bhikṣu Hall.

[The Master] descends. He assembles the bhikṣus and arranges them in order according to their seniority in the precepts. He appoints two bhikṣus by rotation: one to hold incense and one to strike the *qing*.
They enter the *ācārya*’s quarters to welcome the *ācārya* to the seat. Upon his arrival, he leads the bhikṣus in performing three prostrations.
If the *ācārya* is a bodhisattva of venerable seniority (*bahu-varṣa*), it is not necessary for him to thank the assembly; however, if he is a [junior] bhikṣu, he should then offer thanks.
Assembly. As in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, [the procedure] is the same from beginning to end: welcoming, inviting, attending to the seat, and offering praise).

Regarding the True Dharma of the Chan School: without the precepts there is no protection; one must maintain them with steadfast purity to preserve the consciousness of the mind-king. One’s appearance and conduct should be gentle and kind.
Majestic in appearance, he brings benefit and salvation; the fragrance of his precepts gives rise to incense.
